questions.prompt: What does the CAP theorem actually say?

options.text: A distributed system can only ever have two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability
Consistency and availability are impossible together, always
Partitions never happen in practice

questions.explanation: CAP is specifically about behavior during a partition: you must sacrifice either consistency or availability while partitioned. The rest of the time you can have both.

questions.prompt: Why is 'pick 2 of 3' a misleading way to state CAP?

options.text: Because consistency is never achievable
Because partition tolerance isn't optional for a distributed system, so the real choice is C vs A during a partition
Because availability is always chosen
Because there are actually four properties

questions.explanation: Networks fail, so a distributed system must tolerate partitions. You don't trade away P; you choose C or A when a partition occurs.

questions.prompt: During a partition, how does an AP system behave?

options.text: It refuses requests to stay consistent
It answers requests from reachable nodes, possibly returning stale data
It shuts down entirely
It guarantees the latest data on every read

questions.explanation: An AP system favors availability: it answers from whatever nodes are reachable, accepting possibly stale data, and reconciles once the partition heals.

questions.prompt: A teammate says 'our distributed database is CA — consistent and available, no partition tolerance.' What's wrong?

options.text: Nothing, CA is the best choice
You can't opt out of partitions in a distributed system, so CA isn't a meaningful choice — you must pick CP or AP
CA means the system is always down
CA only applies to single-node caches

questions.explanation: Partitions are unavoidable in a distributed system, so 'giving up P' isn't real. The system must decide CP or AP for partition behavior.

questions.prompt: What does PACELC add beyond CAP?

options.text: It removes the need to choose during a partition
It adds the normal-operation trade-off: Else (no partition), choose Latency or Consistency
It proves partitions never happen
It says availability is always best

questions.explanation: PACELC: if Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency — capturing that strong consistency costs latency even without partitions.

questions.prompt: In the CAP theorem, what does 'C' (consistency) specifically mean?

options.text: The ACID integrity constraints of a transaction
Linearizability — every read sees the most recent write
That data is encrypted
That the cache is warm

questions.explanation: CAP's C is linearizability, a recency guarantee — distinct from ACID's C, which is about application integrity constraints.
